analysis.one_liner: Bans unconscionably excessive prices for essential goods during the COVID-19 emergency.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee hearing or a vote in the House before the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made it illegal to charge 'unconscionably excessive' prices for food, medicine, cleaning supplies, personal protective equipment, and certain services while the COVID-19 public health emergency was in effect. It defined excessive by comparing a price to what the same seller charged before the emergency, while letting sellers pass along genuinely higher costs. The Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general could both enforce the ban and seek penalties and refunds for consumers.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary consumers buying pandemic necessities — masks, hand sanitizer, cleaning products, medical supplies, and groceries — who faced sudden markups when demand spiked. States and Indian Tribes also gained a federal backstop they could enforce in court on behalf of their residents, alongside their own price-gouging laws.

how_it_helps.text: Makes it unlawful during the declared COVID-19 emergency to sell any good or service at a price that is unconscionably excessive and reflects the seller using the emergency to raise prices unreasonably [S3].

Covers the goods households most needed during the pandemic: food, water, hygiene products, personal protective equipment, medical and testing supplies, disinfectants, plus healthcare, cleaning, and delivery services [S3].

Lets both the Federal Trade Commission and every state attorney general enforce the ban, allowing states to win civil penalties, restitution, and damages for their residents; the bill explicitly leaves all stronger state and local price-gouging laws in place [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Sellers — retailers, wholesalers, and online marketplaces — that raised prices sharply during the emergency would face federal enforcement, civil penalties, and restitution claims. Honest sellers who only passed on real cost increases were protected by an explicit safe harbor.

drawbacks.text: A federal ceiling on emergency prices can blunt the incentive to bring scarce goods to market quickly; the bill tries to manage this by letting sellers recover additional costs, lost sales, and added risk, but the 'unconscionably excessive' standard is vague enough to invite costly litigation [S3].

The bill creates dual enforcement by the FTC and state attorneys general, and while it bars duplicate state suits against a defendant already named in an FTC case, overlapping investigations could still burden small sellers who raised prices for legitimate reasons [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the specific window of a declared emergency, the benefit to consumers of stopping opportunistic markups on necessities outweighs the cost, which falls only on sellers charging far above their pre-emergency prices after accounting for real cost increases. The temporary duration and the cost-based safe harbor make the design reasonably careful; the main downside is the vagueness of the standard and added compliance burden for sellers.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee on the day it was introduced and sat there with no hearing, markup, or floor vote for the rest of the Congress.

narrative.text: Representative Janice Schakowsky introduced the bill on April 7, 2020, with five original cosponsors, about a month after COVID-19 was declared a nationwide public health emergency [S3].
It was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day, and that was the bill's final action in the 116th Congress [S5].
Thirty-one House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republican cosponsor joined [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Sellers that raised prices sharply during the pandemic were better off, because no federal price-gouging ban ever took effect and enforcement stayed with the patchwork of state laws. Consumers got no federal protection.

for.name: Rep. Janice Schakowsky
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited five colleagues as original cosponsors.

for.name: 31 of 231 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Rep. Frank Pallone, chairman of the committee it was referred to.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on April 7, 2020 and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the remainder of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 31 cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican signed on; no votes were ever taken, so the partisan split is visible only in sponsorship. Even the Democratic chairman of the receiving committee, who cosponsored the bill, never brought it to a hearing.

industries.industry: Retailers, wholesalers, and online marketplaces selling pandemic essentials
industries.note: The bill would have exposed any seller charging unconscionably excessive prices for food, hygiene products, protective equipment, and related services to FTC enforcement and state attorney general suits with penalties and consumer restitution. Its gain for sellers — freedom to mark up scarce necessities — is exactly the consumer's cost.

industries.industry: Medical supply and personal protective equipment distributors
industries.note: PPE, respirators, medical and testing supplies are explicitly covered, so distributors that marked up scarce gear during shortages would face federal liability. Consumers who needed the gear would have paid pre-emergency-style prices instead.
